title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the right small word, every time

questions.prompt: Complete this note from a young cook: "___ a long shift, but the hotel is proud of ___ kitchen."
questions.explanation: "It's" is the short form of "it is", while "its" is the possessive that stands before a noun and takes no apostrophe, so the note reads It's ... its. "Its ... it's" swaps the two and opens the note with a possessive that owns nothing. "It's ... it's" plants "it is" in front of "kitchen", and "Its ... its" leaves the first half of the note with no verb at all.

questions.prompt: Which line from the school noticeboard is correct English?

options.text: The cookery exam is at Friday, on eight o'clock, in April.
The cookery exam is in Friday, at eight o'clock, on April.
The cookery exam is on Friday, at eight o'clock, in April.
The cookery exam is on Friday, in eight o'clock, at April.

questions.explanation: Time zooms out from the clock to the month: a clock time takes "at", a day of the week takes "on" and a month standing on its own takes "in", which gives "The cookery exam is on Friday, at eight o'clock, in April." The three other lines shuffle the same prepositions and each one breaks the scale somewhere: a day of the week never follows "at" or "in", eight o'clock never follows "on" or "in", and a month alone never follows "at" or "on".

questions.prompt: Complete: "The new waiters ___ their manager, and they often ___ their first evening in the hotel."
questions.explanation: These two verbs travel everywhere with their own preposition and never change it, which gives listen to ... think about (think of would be just as correct here, but it is not on offer). "listen at" borrows the preposition of "look at", although listen keeps to in every sentence, and "think to" copies a preposition from another language onto a verb that takes about or of, never to.

options.text: Salma goes home at nine, and her sister keeps a plate for her.
Salma goes home at nine, and her sister keeps a plate to her.
Salma goes to home at nine, and her sister keeps a plate for her.
Salma goes to home at nine, and her sister keeps a plate to her.

questions.explanation: "Home" takes no preposition after "go", and a plate kept for somebody uses "for", the preposition of the person something is meant for: "Salma goes home at nine, and her sister keeps a plate for her." Both lines built on "goes to home" add a preposition that "home" refuses, and both lines built on "keeps a plate to her" turn something meant for Salma into a direction.

questions.prompt: Ines writes about her aunt: "She borrowed money from the bank to buy her first oven, and she paid the bank back in five years." Which word of the lesson names the money she borrowed?
questions.explanation: "a loan" is right: a loan is money you borrow and must pay back, which is exactly what Ines's aunt did with the bank. "a struggle" is a hard fight or effort, not a sum of money; "freedom" is being able to choose for yourself; and "a wedding" is the ceremony where two people marry.

questions.prompt: Complete this note with the right pronouns: "My parents opened the shop in 1998. Every summer ___ ask my brother and ___ to serve the customers, and we do it for ___ all through August."
questions.explanation: A subject pronoun opens the sentence before the verb, an object pronoun follows the verb — even inside "my brother and ___" — and the object form is compulsory after the preposition for, which gives they ... me ... them. "they ... I ... them" keeps the subject form I where the verb ask needs an object; "them ... me ... they" starts the sentence with an object form; and "they ... me ... they" leaves a subject form after for.
